section_summary: This section documents internal political affairs and cabinet crises in Japan from October 1930 through December 1931, focusing on fallout from the London Naval Treaty and the onset of the Manchurian Incident. It chronicles the resignation of Navy Minister Takarabe, the attempted assassination of Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi by an Aikokusha nationalist, Baron Kijuro Shidehara's temporary premiership, and the subsequent formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet following Hamaguchi's decline and death. The documents detail escalating cabinet instability driven by Home Minister Kisaburo Adachi's intrigues for a coalition government, insubordination by military authorities in Mukden, and the final collapse of the Wakatsuki ministry, leading to the installation of Tsuyoshi Inukai's Seiyukai Cabinet.

subfiles.about: Reports the resignation of Navy Minister Takarabe following ratification of the London Naval Treaty and the appointment of Admiral Abo as his successor.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that Admiral Takarabe, Minister of the Navy and delegate to the London Naval Conference, has resigned following the treaty's ratification. Admiral Abo, chief technical adviser to the Japanese delegation, is named to succeed him. Forbes notes that Takarabe's resignation was widely rumored and anticipated, and he does not expect serious political consequences to follow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 184 from Tokyo regarding Resignation of Navy Minister Takarabe

subfiles.about: Confirms and analyzes the resignation of Navy Minister Takarabe and the appointment of Admiral Abo in the context of naval replenishment budget controversies.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes elaborates on the resignation of Admiral Takarabe and the selection of Admiral Abo as Minister of Marine. The despatch quotes the Jiji Shimpo, which attributed Takarabe's departure to his responsibility for promoting the unachievable 'three fundamental principles' before accepting conference concessions. The Tokyo Nichi Nichi and other political figures criticized the resignation as premature given unresolved disputes over naval replenishment funds. Forbes suggests the government chose Abo because his standing within the Navy may facilitate acceptance of a compromise replenishment program.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 17: Resignation of Admiral Takarabe and Appointment of Admiral Abo as Minister of Marine

subfiles.about: Urgent initial report that Prime Minister Hamaguchi was shot and seriously wounded at Tokyo Station.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Dooman reports urgently that Premier Osachi Hamaguchi was shot and seriously wounded on the morning of November 14, 1930.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 214 from Tokyo Reporting Shooting of Premier Hamaguchi

subfiles.about: Details Premier Hamaguchi's abdominal bullet wound, hemorrhage, emergency medical treatment, and the immediate arrest of the assailant.
subfiles.summary: Dooman provides follow-up details on the shooting of Prime Minister Hamaguchi, noting that the bullet struck his abdomen without exiting and that initial attempts to extract it failed. Considerable alarm was caused by profuse bleeding that could not immediately be checked. The assailant, identified as a member of an organization of reactionary political adventurers, was arrested immediately at the scene.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 216 from Tokyo on Premier Hamaguchi's Condition and Assailant's Arrest

subfiles.about: Instructs the Embassy to convey the condolences and sympathy of the United States Government and Secretary of State to the Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs the Embassy in Tokyo to inform the Minister for Foreign Affairs that the United States Government and the Secretary of State personally are profoundly shocked by the attempted assassination of Prime Minister Hamaguchi. The message expresses earnest hopes that Hamaguchi's life, which has contributed so nobly to world peace, may be spared to his country.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 206 to Tokyo Expressing Sympathy for Premier Hamaguchi

subfiles.about: Reports Foreign Minister Shidehara's gratitude for American sympathy, Hamaguchi's favorable post-operation recovery, and pending Cabinet leadership decisions.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reports that Foreign Minister Shidehara conveyed warm thanks for the American message of sympathy regarding Premier Hamaguchi. Shidehara reported optimistically that Hamaguchi responded favorably to his surgical operation with little likelihood of complications. The telegram notes that the Cabinet will decide that morning whether to designate an acting Prime Minister pro tempore.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 217 from Tokyo on Premier Hamaguchi's Condition and Cabinet Deliberations

subfiles.about: Reports the expected appointment of Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara as Prime Minister pro tempore.
subfiles.summary: Dooman reports that Baron Kijuro Shidehara is scheduled to be appointed Prime Minister pro tempore during the incapacitation of Premier Hamaguchi.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 218 from Tokyo Reporting Appointment of Baron Shidehara as Prime Minister Pro Tempore

subfiles.about: Internal State Department routing memorandum summarizing the contents of Ambassador Forbes's Despatch No. 58 for Assistant Secretary Castle.
subfiles.from: R. S. M. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: An internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum calls Assistant Secretary William R. Castle's attention to Tokyo Despatch No. 58. The memorandum summarizes the despatch's contents, noting that it details the attack on Premier Hamaguchi, embassy representations, Minseito internal politics, Shidehara's appointment as temporary Premier, and background on the Patriotic Society.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 58 Regarding Attack on Premier Hamaguchi

subfiles.about: Comprehensive account of the shooting of Premier Hamaguchi, emergency medical actions, internal Minseito party rivalries, Shidehara's acting premiership, and ultra-nationalist societies.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes provides a detailed narrative of the shooting of Premier Hamaguchi at Tokyo Station on November 14, 1930, by a young reactionary assailant, including emergency blood transfusions and operations at Tokyo Imperial University Hospital. The despatch analyzes Minseito factional dynamics between Home Minister Adachi and Railways Minister Egi, explaining how Baron Shidehara was selected as non-partisan Prime Minister pro tempore with the backing of elder statesman Wakatsuki and the Emperor. It also exposes the influence of right-wing nationalist groups such as the Patriotic Society and Black Dragon Society under Mitsuru Toyama, linking the attack to resentment over the London Naval Treaty. Forbes notes widespread public and press condemnation of the crime and praise for Hamaguchi's fiscal policies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 58: Attempted Assassination of Premier Hamaguchi and Political Developments

subfiles.about: Transmits a formal diplomatic note of thanks from Japanese Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara for the United States Government's expressions of sympathy.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes transmits a formal diplomatic note dated November 19, 1930, from Baron Kijuro Shidehara, Minister for Foreign Affairs. Shidehara conveys the profound gratitude of the Imperial Japanese Government and himself to the United States Government and the Secretary of State for their warm messages of sympathy following the attack on Premier Hamaguchi.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 69: Transmission of Note of Thanks from Foreign Minister Shidehara

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 36 reporting on the shooting of Premier Hamaguchi, the identification of assailant Tomeo Sagoya, and the extremist background of the Aikokusha.
subfiles.summary: Prefaced by cross-reference sheet 894.002/154, this extract from Political Report No. 36 recounts the shooting of Premier Hamaguchi at Tokyo Central Station as he departed for military manoeuvres in Okayama Prefecture. After the lifting of press censorship, the assailant was identified as twenty-three-year-old Tomeo Sagoya of the Aikokusha (Patriotic Society). The report details Sagoya's background as a vagrant and bandit in Manchuria with a criminal history, and examines Aikokusha leader Ainosuke Iwata's prior conviction for the 1913 assassination of Foreign Office bureau chief Moritaro Abe. It also draws parallels to the 1921 assassination of Prime Minister Takashi Hara.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 74 (Extract): Attempted Assassination of Premier Hamaguchi and Sketch of Culprit Tomeo Sagoya

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 37 discussing Premier Hamaguchi's slow convalescence, impending Diet session concerns, and legal proceedings against Sagoya and his accomplices.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/155, this extract from Political Report No. 37 notes that Hamaguchi's incomplete recovery from his wounds created serious political unrest regarding his attendance at the January Diet session. Police arrested Yoshikatsu Matsuki as an accomplice and Aikokusha leader Ainosuke Iwata for firearms violations, subsequently lifting the press embargo. Investigations revealed that Sagoya had plotted the assassination since May 1930 over economic depression and unemployment, obtaining Iwata's revolver through Matsuki. The report emphasizes Iwata's vocal opposition to the London Naval Treaty and Hamaguchi's foreign diplomacy.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 107 (Extract): Premier Hamaguchi's Health and Legal Proceedings Against Sagoya and Accomplices

subfiles.about: Reports the en bloc resignation of the Hamaguchi Cabinet due to Premier Hamaguchi's ill health and the expectation that Baron Wakatsuki will form a new ministry.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/156, Telegram No. 50 reports that the Hamaguchi Cabinet has resigned en bloc due to the failing health of Prime Minister Hamaguchi. Ambassador Forbes reports that former Prime Minister Reijiro Wakatsuki will be asked to form a new Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 50 from Tokyo Reporting Resignation of Hamaguchi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports that Baron Wakatsuki is forming a new Minseito Cabinet with minimal personnel changes and continuity in foreign and financial policies.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/157, Telegram No. 55 reports that newly created Baron Wakatsuki is forming a new Cabinet with personnel largely identical to the Hamaguchi administration. Shidehara remains at the Foreign Office and Inouye at Finance, while the Ministers of War, Commerce, and Overseas Affairs retire voluntarily. No changes in policy are anticipated as the ministry remains strongly dominated by the Minseito.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 55 from Tokyo on Formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Detailed political analysis of Premier Hamaguchi's resignation, factional rivalries within the Minseito, the compromise selection of Baron Wakatsuki, and public and press reaction.
subfiles.summary: Prefaced by cross-reference sheet 894.002/158, Ambassador Forbes reports on the succession from Hamaguchi to Baron Wakatsuki following Hamaguchi's resignation due to an impending operation and physical exhaustion from Diet debates. The despatch analyzes the intense internal Minseito struggle between Home Minister Adachi and War Minister General Ugaki for party leadership, which threatened party unity until party manager Koizumi and railway head Sengoku engineered a compromise behind Wakatsuki. In the reconstructed Cabinet, General Minami becomes War Minister, Shuzo Hara heads Overseas Affairs, and Yukio Sakurauchi takes Commerce, while foreign and financial portfolios remain unchanged. Wakatsuki announced adherence to Hamaguchi's retrenchment and no-loan policies, earning cautious confidence from the press and markets.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 210: Resignation of Hamaguchi and Formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 41 reviewing Hamaguchi's resignation, Wakatsuki's emergence from retirement, and new ministerial appointments.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/159, this extract from Political Report No. 41 reviews the resignation of Premier Hamaguchi following doctors' warnings that another operation was required. Baron Wakatsuki reluctantly accepted the leadership of the Minseito and the premiership to avert a divisive factional rift between party rivals. The report outlines new appointments including War Minister General Minami, Overseas Affairs Minister Hara, and Commerce Minister Sakurauchi, reaffirming policy adherence to the Hamaguchi administration's program.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 216 (Extract): Overview of Hamaguchi's Resignation and the New Wakatsuki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 45 reporting the death of former Premier Hamaguchi from his gunshot wounds and the status of assassin Tomeo Sagoya's trial.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/160, this extract from Political Report No. 45 reports that former Premier 'Lion' Hamaguchi died on August 26, 1931, nine and a half months after being shot. An autopsy revealed the bullet embedded in bone, with observers noting that opposition pressure requiring Hamaguchi's physical attendance at the Diet critically worsened his condition. Assassin Tomeo Sagoya remains detained in Toyotama Prison awaiting trial after the conclusion of preliminary judicial proceedings.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 324 (Extract): Death of Former Premier Osachi Hamaguchi

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing an Undersecretary memorandum regarding an extremist plot against Premier Wakatsuki, Foreign Minister Shidehara, Count Makino, and Finance Minister Inouye.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet (894.002/161) referencing a memorandum dated November 14, 1931, by Undersecretary William R. Castle, Jr., filed under 793.94/2722. The referenced document details an assassination plot against Prime Minister Wakatsuki, Foreign Minister Shidehara, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Count Makino, and Finance Minister Inouye.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.002/161: Plot Against Wakatsuki, Shidehara, Makino, and Inouye

subfiles.about: Reports diplomatic corps assessments advising against League pressure on Japan, rumors of Cabinet changes, possible coalition formulas, and extensive military troop movements toward Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/162, Telegram No. 223 conveys opinions from the Dutch and Norwegian Ministers warning that external pressure will consolidate Japanese nationalist sentiment and empower the military. Forbes analyzes rumors of an impending Cabinet change driven by League diplomacy, military defiance since September 18, and financial strain, assessing three possibilities: an Adachi-Tokonami coalition, a Seiyukai government, or a reorganized Wakatsuki coalition. The telegram highlights strict press bans on troop deployments and reports Colonel McIlroy's observations of heavy rail troop movements and orchestrated war enthusiasm toward Mukden.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 223 from Tokyo on Diplomatic Views, Cabinet Instability, and Military Mobilization

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram regarding Japanese press reports of a plot to kill Foreign Minister Shidehara and other officials.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet (894.002/163) referencing Telegram No. 235 sent from Japan on November 19, 1931, filed under 793.94/2758. The referenced telegram reports on newspaper disclosures of a plot to assassinate Foreign Minister Shidehara and other prominent statesmen.
subfiles.title: Document File Note 894.002/163: Newspaper Report of Plot to Kill Shidehara and Others

subfiles.about: Biographical notice informing the Department of State of the death of Baron Ryuichi Kuki, former Japanese Minister to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Professor Shigeo Yamanouchi of the University of Chicago informs the Department of State of the death of Baron Ryuichi Kuki on August 18, 1931, at his villa in Kamakura. The letter provides a detailed curriculum vitae outlining Kuki's distinguished career as Dean of Tokyo Imperial University, Minister to Washington during the Arthur and Cleveland administrations, and Senior Member of the Privy Council. It lists surviving family members, including his grandson and successor Baron Ryuichiro Kuki, and records funeral arrangements in Tokyo and burial in Sanda, Hyogo Prefecture.
subfiles.title: Letter from Shigeo Yamanouchi Announcing the Death of Baron Ryuichi Kuki

subfiles.about: Letter from the Division of Protocol acknowledging receipt of the announcement of the death of former Minister Baron Ryuichi Kuki and expressing condolence.
subfiles.summary: Warren D. Robbins, Chief of the Division of Protocol, writes to Mr. Shigeo Yamanouchi at the University of Chicago acknowledging his letter announcing the death of Baron Ryuichi Kuki. Robbins expresses appreciation for bringing the lamented fact to the Department's attention and reiterates the United States Government's deepest regrets.
subfiles.title: Letter of Condolence to Shigeo Yamanouchi on the Death of Baron Ryuichi Kuki

subfiles.about: Reports the temporary easing of the Cabinet crisis, Home Minister Adachi's lull in coalition agitation, and growing friction caused by insurgent young army officers in Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/165, Telegram No. 247 reports that the immediate Cabinet crisis appears to have passed as Home Minister Adachi has temporarily ceased his coalition maneuvers. Forbes notes serious tension between conservative military heads (the Minister of War and Chief of Staff) and rebellious younger officers issuing unauthorized, contradictory press statements in Mukden. Dr. Teusler and senior Japanese figures expressed deep concern that radical elements in the military have gotten out of hand, paralleled by similar unauthorized press releases from civilian ministries.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 247 from Tokyo on Temporary Passing of Cabinet Crisis and Army Insubordination

subfiles.about: Comprehensive analysis of the rumored fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet, Adachi-Tokonami coalition intrigues, alternative premiers, and prospects for an Imperial Rescript to restrain the military.
subfiles.summary: Prefaced by cross-reference sheet 894.002/166, Ambassador Forbes analyzes the precarious position of the Wakatsuki Cabinet despite its Diet majority, amid public criticism over Manchurian military aggression, League disputes, and economic policies. Forbes examines backroom negotiations between disgruntled Home Minister Adachi and Seiyukai leader Tokonami to establish a coalition government, noting that unprincipled intrigues face opposition from Genro Prince Saionji and Privy Seal Count Makino. Potential prime ministerial successors discussed include Seiyukai leader Tsuyoshi Inukai, Baron Tatsuo Yamamoto, and Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma. Furthermore, Forbes highlights confidential reports that court advisers may seek an Imperial Rescript from the Emperor to reassert civilian authority over the military.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 396: Comprehensive Analysis of Impending Cabinet Crisis, Party Factions, and Imperial Rescript Prospects

subfiles.about: Reports Prime Minister Wakatsuki's resignation to the Emperor due to Home Minister Adachi's coalition demands and reviews probable successors.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/167, Telegram No. 258 reports that Baron Wakatsuki tendered the Cabinet's resignation to the Emperor on December 11, 1931. Forbes emphasizes that the collapse resulted from internal political maneuvers by Home Minister Adachi demanding a coalition government, rather than government policies or Manchurian events. Speculation on the premiership focuses on whether Wakatsuki will be asked to reconstitute the ministry or if opposition Seiyukai leader Tsuyoshi Inukai will be summoned.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 258 from Tokyo Reporting Resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports that opposition Seiyukai President Tsuyoshi Inukai has been summoned to the Imperial Palace to form a new Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Prefaced by cross-reference sheet 894.002/168, Telegram No. 259 reports that diplomatic representations are deferred pending the appointment of a new Foreign Minister following the Cabinet's fall. Forbes confirms that Tsuyoshi Inukai, President of the Seiyukai, was summoned to the Imperial Palace to be entrusted with forming the next ministry.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 259 from Tokyo on Summoning of Tsuyoshi Inukai to Form a Cabinet

subfiles.about: Lists the ministerial appointments in the newly established Seiyukai Cabinet formed by Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Prefaced by cross-reference sheet 894.002/169, Telegram No. 261 reports the ministerial roster of the newly formed Inukai Cabinet. Premier Inukai assumes the concurrent portfolio of Acting Foreign Minister pending the return of Ambassador Kenkichi Yoshizawa from France. Other key appointments include Tokugoro Nakahashi (Home Affairs), Korekiyo Takahashi (Finance), Lt. Gen. Sadao Araki (War), Admiral Mineo Osumi (Marine), Kisaburo Suzuki (Justice), Ichiro Hatoyama (Education), Teijiro Yamamoto (Agriculture), Yonezo Maeda (Commerce), Chuzo Mitsuchi (Communications), and Toyosuke Hata (Overseas Affairs).
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 261 from Tokyo Reporting Ministerial Appointments in the Inukai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Extract from Political Report No. 48 discussing domestic political unrest and party friction caused by Home Minister Adachi's unauthorized public advocacy for a coalition cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Accompanied by cross-reference sheet 894.002/170, this extract from Political Report No. 48 details the severe embarrassment caused to the Wakatsuki Government by rumors of an impending Cabinet change. Home Minister Kisaburo Adachi caused a major sensation and party crisis by publicly advocating a national coalition government without consulting his Minseito colleagues. The report highlights intense dissatisfaction with Shidehara's diplomacy and Inouye's financial policies, discussing whether Adachi acted out of personal ambition to claim the premiership or revived an idea earlier considered by Premier Wakatsuki.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 404 (Extract): Internal Political Friction and Adachi's Coalition Maneuvers
